name: Tomás's brain thermostat during a fever

parameters.label: How hard his immune system is fighting
parameters.explain: Fighting germs releases signals that raise the brain's temperature set point — the temperature the body tries to reach.

parameters.label: Hours since the fever started
parameters.explain: The twist dial: early on, his body is below the new set point, so he feels cold and shivers. When the fever eases, his body is above it, so he feels hot and sweats.

parameters.label: Blankets
parameters.explain: Test the 'blankets are overheating him' idea: blankets hold heat in, so he warms up to the set point faster — but they don't move the set point.

parameters.label: Room temperature
parameters.explain: Test the 'the room is cold' idea: a cooler room adds a little shivering, but the fever comes from inside, not from the room.

parameters.label: His normal temperature
parameters.explain: Healthy people usually sit somewhere between about 97.8 °F and 99 °F.

parameters.label: Hours until the fever eases
parameters.explain: When the immune signals fade, the set point drops back to normal and the body has to shed its extra heat.

overlay.caption: germs → immune signals turn the brain's thermostat up → shiver to heat up; thermostat down → sweat

explain.summary: When Tomás's immune system fights the germs from his cold, it sends signals that turn up his brain's thermostat. His body is now colder than the new setting, so he feels freezing and shivers to make heat — even though his forehead is hot. Hours later the fight eases, the thermostat drops back, and now his body is too warm, so he sweats.
rules: The harder the immune system fights, the higher the brain's set point goes.
Body temperature follows the set point, but about an hour behind.
While body temperature is below the set point he feels cold and shivers.
When the set point drops back, body temperature is above it and he sweats.
Blankets and room temperature change how fast he warms or cools — not the set point.

source.fact: A fever happens when signalling chemicals (pyrogens) raise the body's temperature set point. A moderate fever is about 100.6–102.2 °F.
In a fever, the body's thermostat resets at a higher temperature, mostly because of an infection.
Chills are the body's way of raising its core temperature; shivering muscles contract and relax, which warms the body. Many people feel chilled when they have a fever.
Fever is an important part of the body's defence against infection. Body temperature is usually highest in the evening, and someone with chills should not be bundled up.
Normal body temperature in healthy adults is generally between 97.8 °F and 99 °F.

choice.what: The set point rises 0.45 °F for each step of 'fight'
choice.why: A fight of 7 gives a set point near 101.7 °F — a moderate fever — matching the 101 °F Tomás's thermometer reads as he is still warming up.

choice.what: Body temperature lags the set point by about an hour
choice.why: Warming takes time; the lag is what creates the cold, shivery phase. Blankets and a warm room shorten it.

choice.what: Shivering and sweating depend on the gap between body temperature and set point
choice.why: That's how a thermostat works: below the setting it heats, above the setting it cools.

choice.what: A cooler room adds a little extra shivering
choice.why: A cold room takes heat away faster, but it can't create a fever by itself.

illustrative: The 0–10 'fight' scale, the 0–10 shivering and sweating scales, and Tomás's four hours until the fever eases are teaching values.
Tomás is fictional; his normal temperature (98.6 °F) is a typical value.
provenance.studying: Exactly how much a fever helps the body fight different germs is still being researched.

does: Shows a fever as the brain's thermostat being turned up, not the body losing control
Shows why someone with a hot forehead can feel cold and shiver
Shows sweating when the fever eases and the thermostat goes back down
doesnt: Measure anyone's temperature or say what to do about a fever
Include high or dangerous fevers; the model stays in the moderate range
Model the germs themselves or how long a real cold lasts
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: A high fever, a fever that lasts more than a couple of days, or feeling very unwell is a reason to tell an adult.
